Explain what lean attacks, the eight wastes, value-added work and flow.
Name the project roles, from sponsor and champion to each belt, and what each is accountable for.
Distinguish improvement, cross-functional, self-directed and virtual teams and when each fits.
Recognize forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning, and what a team needs at each.
Use brainstorming, multivoting and nominal group technique to reach a decision.
Choose how and how often to communicate with team members and stakeholders.
Choose and read the basic quality tools: Pareto, histogram, check sheet, cause and effect, scatter, run chart, flowchart.
Calculate and interpret DPU, DPMO, RTY, sigma level and the cost of poor quality.
Gather customer needs and turn them into measurable critical-to-quality requirements.
Judge which candidate projects are worth doing and scope them so they can be finished.
Identify stakeholders, their influence and stance, and how to engage each.
Build a SIPOC and map a process at the right level of detail.
Explain how suppliers and customers along the chain affect the process and its quality.
Write a charter: problem statement, scope, baseline, goal, team and sponsor sign-off.
Plan who hears what, by which channel and how often, through the project.
Break the work down, sequence it and set milestones.
Read and use a Gantt chart, work breakdown structure and critical path.
Explain what a tollgate review checks before a project moves to the next phase.
Calculate and interpret mean, median, mode, range and standard deviation.
Write a data collection plan with operational definitions, sources and frequency.
Tell attribute from variable data, and the nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio scales apart.
Choose sampling and collection methods such as check sheets, surveys and random or stratified samples.

bank: I.A
The primary aim of Six Sigma is to reduce:
Cycle time
Variation
Inspection
Inventory

Six Sigma attacks variation: output differing from unit to unit and over time. Shorter cycle time, less inventory and less inspection can all follow from a more consistent process, but they are consequences rather than the target; cycle time and inventory are lean’s primary concerns.
std
I.A
DMAIC stands for:
Design, model, assess, implement, check
Define, model, apply, inspect, correct
Detect, measure, act, improve, close
Define, measure, analyze, improve, control
The five phases run in that order for a reason: measurement precedes analysis so the cause is found from data rather than decided in advance, and control follows improvement so the gain holds.
std
II.B.1
A project charter should state all of the following except:
The measure of success
The scope
The root cause
The problem

The cause is what the project will establish, and a charter that names it has decided the answer before the measure phase. Problem, scope and success measure all have to exist at the start for the project to be assessable.
std
I.C
The role of a Green Belt typically differs from that of a Black Belt in that a Green Belt:
Is not expected to use any statistical tools
Reports project results directly to the customer
Works projects part time alongside a normal job
Owns the quality management system for the site

Green Belts run improvement projects alongside their operational role, which is what makes them numerous and close to the work. Both roles use statistical tools; the difference is depth and time available.
std
I.E.2
Scrap and rework found before the product ships are classed as which cost of quality category?
Appraisal
External failure
Internal failure
Prevention

Failures found before the product reaches the customer are internal failure costs; those found after are external failure. Together they are the cost of poor quality. Appraisal is the cost of checking and prevention the cost of stopping defects happening.
std
II.A.2
A project whose scope is "improve the plant" should be:
Narrowed until the problem is measurable
Approved, as improvement is always valuable
Split among several belts
Escalated to management
A scope that cannot be measured cannot be shown to have succeeded, and it will expand indefinitely. Narrowing to a specific problem with a baseline is what makes a project completable.
std
I.C
The sponsor of a Six Sigma project is principally responsible for:
Removing obstacles and releasing resources
Facilitating the team’s weekly meetings
Writing and maintaining the control plan
Collecting and analyzing the project data

A sponsor supplies what the team cannot get for itself: time, access and decisions above the team’s authority. A sponsor who cannot release people has not sponsored anything, whatever the charter says.
std
I.B
Lean and Six Sigma differ in that lean primarily attacks:
Waste
Cost
Variation
Defects

Lean attacks waste — waiting, transport, inventory, motion, overproduction, overprocessing, defects. Six Sigma attacks variation. Applying the wrong one works hard and improves nothing, and applying lean to an unstable process makes it worse.
std
I.E.2
Allowing for the conventional 1.5 sigma shift, a process operating at six sigma produces approximately:
340 defects per million opportunities
34 defects per million opportunities
3.4 defects per million opportunities
3.4 percent of units defective

The conventional figure assumes a 1.5 sigma long-term shift in the mean, which is why it is 3.4 rather than the two-per-billion a static normal distribution would give. The shift allowance is part of the convention rather than an error.
std
IV.E.2
A process is described as "stable but not capable". This means:
It is out of statistical control most of the time
Its measurement system is not adequate for the job
It is predictable but out of specification
It meets the specification, but unpredictably

Stability and capability are separate questions. A stable process is predictable and may predictably produce nonconforming output; the response is a process change rather than tighter control, because it is already doing its best.
std
I.E.2
A defect and a defective differ in that:
A defect applies only to attribute-type data
A defect is found only at final inspection
A defective is simply a more serious defect
A defective unit has at least one defect
A defect is one nonconformity; a defective is a unit that fails because it has one or more of them. A unit can have several defects and still be counted once as defective.
std
II.A.4
A SIPOC diagram is used to:
Scope a process at a high level
Rank causes by how often they occur
Compute capability
Confirm the root cause of a problem
SIPOC names suppliers, inputs, process, outputs and customers so that a mapping exercise has a boundary before the detail starts. Without it, mapping expands until it is abandoned.
std
II.A.1
Rather than asking customers for a specification, voice of the customer interviews should focus on:
The price they would be willing to pay
Only the complaints they have made before
The problem the product solves for them
What competitors are offering them now

Customers describe solutions more readily than needs, so a request for a specification returns their guess at an answer. Asking about the problem produces the need, which may have a cheaper or better solution than the one they proposed.
std
II.A.1
A critical-to-quality characteristic is:
A measurable feature tied to a customer need
A feature named in the governing industry standard
The tightest tolerance shown on the drawing
Any feature of the product that can be measured

CTQ links a customer requirement to something the process can measure and control. A tight tolerance that no requirement depends on is a cost rather than a CTQ, and it is one of the commoner sources of unnecessary expense.
std
II.A.1
Kano classifies an attribute customers do not notice when present but complain about when absent as:
Must-be
One-dimensional
Indifferent
Attractive
Must-be attributes produce no satisfaction when met and severe dissatisfaction when missed, which is why improving them beyond adequate returns nothing. Investment there is the classic misallocation.
std
II.A.1
A customer states a need for "faster delivery". The team should first:
Establish what faster would enable for them
Add finished stock so orders ship sooner
Benchmark the delivery times of competitors
Set a goal to cut the lead time by half

The stated need is a solution. Understanding what it enables — predictability, less stock, a shorter cycle of their own — frequently reveals that reliability matters more than speed, which is a different and often cheaper project.
std
II.B.1
A project baseline is needed principally to:
Meet the format the charter requires
Compare performance against competitors
Fix the project’s budget for the year
Show whether the change worked

Without a measurement taken before the change, the comparison afterwards is against a memory. It is the single most common omission in improvement projects and it is unrecoverable once the change is made.
std
II.B.1
A project charter is best signed by:
The customer
The quality manager
The sponsor
The team
The sponsor is the one committing resources and authority, and their signature is what makes the charter more than a statement of intent. Team agreement matters but does not release anybody’s time.
std
II.A.4
A high-level process map at define stage should show:
Every step and decision point in full detail
The cycle time and wait time for every step
Only the steps that add value for the customer
Major steps and where the problem occurs
The define map exists to locate the problem, not to document the process. Detailed mapping belongs in measure and analyze, once the team knows which part of the process to examine.
std
II.B.1
Which scope statement in a project charter is clearest?
Everything the shipping department does
Every product made
From order receipt to shipment
All shipping work during the coming year

A scope bounded by a process start and end point says exactly where the project begins and ends. A department, a time period or a whole product range leaves the process boundaries open, which invites scope creep.
std
II.B.1
A problem statement should not contain:
A quantity
A time period
A location
A proposed cause
A statement containing a cause has ended the investigation before the measure phase. What, where, when and how much are all legitimate; why is what the project exists to establish.
std
III.C.2
A gauge R&R study assesses:
The share of variation due to measurement
How capable the process is against its limits
Whether the drawing tolerance is wide enough
Whether the gauge is calibrated to a standard

Calibration establishes that a gauge reads correctly against a standard; it says nothing about whether two operators get the same answer. A fully calibrated gauge can contribute half the observed variation.
std
III.C.2
A gauge R&R result of 35 percent of total variation is:
Acceptable for non-critical characteristics
Acceptable if the gauge is calibrated
Acceptable
Not acceptable

The usual AIAG guideline is under 10 percent acceptable, 10 to 30 percent conditionally acceptable depending on the application, and over 30 percent unacceptable. At 35 percent the measurement system needs improving before capability figures or control chart signals computed from its data can be trusted, whether or not the gauge is calibrated.
std
III.B.2
Data collected as pass or fail is:
Attribute data
Continuous data
Variable data
Ordinal data

Attribute data is counted; variable data is measured on a scale. Variable data carries far more information per observation, which is why a variables chart detects a shift much sooner than an attributes chart on the same process.
std
I.E.1
A histogram that stops abruptly at a specification limit most likely indicates:
A capable process
Two populations
Measurement error
Sorted output

A truncated shape usually means the tail was removed by inspection, so the histogram shows what survived rather than what was made. Any capability index computed from it describes the sorting rather than the process.
std
I.E.2
Using the defects-per-million method, process sigma is found from:
The control limits
The specification limits and the nominal
Defects, units and opportunities
The sample size and the confidence level

Sigma level is derived from defects per million opportunities, which is why counting opportunities consistently matters. Changing the opportunity count changes the sigma level without changing the process at all.
std
III.C.1
Repeatability refers to variation:
Between different operators measuring one part
In the readings over a long period of time
Across the measurement range of the gauge
Within one operator measuring repeatedly

Repeatability is the gauge itself — one operator, one part, repeated measurements. Reproducibility is the variation between operators, which points at method rather than equipment and is fixed by a written method rather than a new gauge.
std
V.B.2
A run chart is preferable to a control chart when:
The data is attribute rather than variable
You only want to see the data in time order
The sample size is large enough for limits
You need to know if a point is a special cause

A run chart plots the data in time order, usually against the median, and needs no control limits, so it is a quick way to see trends, shifts and cycles. Judging whether a point is a special cause needs the calculated limits of a control chart, and control charts exist for attribute data as well as variable data.
std
III.B.3
Which sampling method risks systematic bias on a five-station machine?
Stratified sampling
Sampling by shift
Every fifth part
Random sampling

Every fifth part on a five-station machine samples one station forever, so the shop looks consistent while one station drifts unmeasured. Systematic sampling fails whenever the interval coincides with a cycle in the process.
std
IV.E.2
Before computing capability, the first check should be:
Process stability
Operator training
Specification width
Sample size

Capability predicts future output, and prediction requires the process to keep doing what it was doing. An index computed across a period containing a tool change and two operators describes a mixture and will not predict next week.
std
I.E.1
A Pareto chart ranked by count rather than cost may mislead when:
The data covers too short a period of time
The categories were defined before collection
All of the defect types cost about the same
A few expensive defects are outnumbered by cheap ones

Forty small defects and three expensive ones rank differently by count and by cost, and the chart drawn decides where the effort goes. Where the costs differ materially, ranking by count sends the project to the wrong place.
std
IV.B
Five whys should continue until:
Exactly five rounds of the question have been asked
A person to blame for the problem has been identified
Everyone on the team agrees with the answer
The answer is something the organization can change

There is nothing magic about five. Stopping at "the operator misread the gauge" gives a cause the organization cannot change; "the gauge displays in millimeters and the drawing is in inches" is fixable and would prevent recurrence.
std
I.E.1
Stratifying defect data by shift, machine and operator is worth doing because:
A total can hide one shift or machine that is failing
It increases the sample size available
It is required by most of the quality standards in use
It makes the Pareto chart simpler and faster to draw

A defect rate of two percent across three shifts may be half a percent on two and five percent on the third, and the aggregate hides the only useful fact. Stratifying takes minutes when each record carries the shift, machine and operator, which is why those fields belong on the check sheet from the start.
std
IV.E.2
A multi-vari study is used to establish:
The single root cause of the defect
Whether variation is within-piece, piece-to-piece or over time
The capability index of the process
The share of variation due to the gauge

Naming which family of variation dominates directs everything afterwards. Time-to-time variation is what control charts detect; within-piece variation points at the operation itself, and the two lead to entirely different projects.
stretch
IV.B
A cause and effect diagram:
Confirms the root cause
Ranks causes by frequency
Tests a hypothesis
Generates candidate causes

A fishbone produces candidates and confirms nothing. It requires no data at all, which is exactly why it appears in meetings that have none — and the step that matters is asking what evidence would distinguish the candidates.
std
IV.F.1
A scatter diagram showing no linear pattern:
Means the sample is too small
Suggests no linear link; a curved one may still exist
Proves the variables are unrelated
Indicates measurement error

A strong curved relationship can show a correlation coefficient near zero, which is why plotting comes before computing. The plot also exposes an outlier driving an apparent correlation, which the coefficient conceals.
std
IV.F.1
Areas with the heaviest inspection also have the highest defect rates. Inspection there was increased after defects rose. The correlation most likely reflects:
Inspection causing the defects
A purely random association
An error in the measurement system
Defects prompting inspection

The causal direction runs the other way: processes known to produce defects get inspected more. Reading the correlation forward would suggest reducing inspection improves quality, which is the kind of conclusion that reaches production.
std
IV.G
A p-value of 0.03 means:
There is a 3 percent chance the null is true
The result will replicate 97 percent of the time
The effect is large
Data this extreme would be unlikely if there were no effect

The p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme given the null, not the probability of the null given the data. It says nothing about the size of the effect, which is the number that decides whether anything is worth doing.
std
IV.G
A study reporting "no significant difference" from a sample of twenty:
Establishes that there is no real difference
Cannot rule out a small real effect
Should be repeated with a smaller sample
Proves the two groups are equivalent

Without a power calculation, a null result from a small sample establishes nothing. An organization concluding a change did nothing, on a study that could not have detected it, has learned nothing and believes it has.
std
IV.G
A hypothesis test comparing four group means should use:
Six pairwise t-tests
Analysis of variance
Four t-tests
A chi-square test

Six pairwise comparisons at five percent each give roughly a 26 percent chance of at least one false positive. ANOVA asks the question once and controls the overall error rate; pairwise comparison follows only if it says yes.
stretch
IV.F.2
A regression shows a significant coefficient and an R-squared of 0.04. This most likely indicates:
A real but nearly useless relationship
A strong, useful predictor of y
An impossible result from a valid analysis
An error in the regression model

With enough data a trivial relationship becomes statistically detectable. R-squared says how much variation the model accounts for, and four percent means the factor is real and explains almost nothing worth acting on.
std
IV.G
Design of experiments is preferred to one-factor-at-a-time testing because it:
Is simpler
Uses fewer runs and detects interactions
Avoids the need for a stable process
Requires no statistics

Two factors that each do little alone but matter together are invisible to sequential testing, because the first is tested at the wrong level of the second. Factorial designs also test each factor several times over within the same runs.
stretch
V.A.2
A piloted improvement should be evaluated:
Whenever the sponsor asks for an update
Once enough time and volume have passed
Immediately after the change is implemented
At the next scheduled internal audit
Measured immediately, results are inflated by attention. The novelty and the extra supervision both wear off, and what survives that is what the change actually produced.
std
IV.A.1
Poka-yoke that prevents an error is preferable to one that detects it because:
It is cheaper
It satisfies the standard
It requires no training
The error cannot occur at all

A preventive device makes the mistake impossible; a detective one catches it after it has happened. Prevention removes the defect and the cost of dealing with it, and neither depends on attention, which fails.
std
V.A.2
A solution that works in a pilot but not at scale most often failed because:
Conditions differed outside the pilot
The operators were trained too thoroughly
The control plan was written too early
The measure changed

A pilot runs with attention, chosen people and a controlled environment. What did not transfer is usually a condition the pilot supplied without anybody noticing, and finding it is more useful than repeating the pilot.
std
IV.A.1
SMED reduces batch size by:
Reducing setup time so smaller batches are economic
Adding capacity at the bottleneck step
Automating the process so that it runs at a higher speed
Holding more inventory between operations to smooth flow

Long setups force large batches because the setup cost must be spread across many parts. Cutting setup time makes smaller batches economic, and the main benefit is less inventory and a shorter feedback loop rather than the hour saved.
std
V.A.2
The purpose of a pilot is principally to:
Lock the solution in so that nobody can change it later
Give the sponsor a result to report upward
Find problems at small scale before rollout
Train every operator in the final method
A pilot tries the solution on a small scale so problems surface while they are still cheap to fix. Treating it as a formality, rather than a test, sends an undiscovered fault into the full rollout.
std
IV.A.1
A line is limited by one constraint step. Making a different, non-constraint step faster will most likely:
Reduce the work in process ahead of the constraint
Leave line output unchanged
Raise line output by about half the gain
Raise line output in proportion to the gain

Output is set by the constraint, so speeding up any other step leaves line output where it was. A faster step upstream of the constraint tends to build more work in process in front of it, not less. Effort pays off at the constraint first.
std
IV.A.1
Before removing buffer stock from a process, the team should establish that the process is:
Documented
Automated
Certified
Stable

Buffer exists because the process is unreliable. Removing it from an unstable process exposes the instability as line stoppages, and the organization concludes lean does not work. Stabilize, then flow.
std
IV.G
A designed experiment run on an unstable process is likely to:
Detect interactions between the factors more easily
Produce more precise estimates of the effects
Require fewer runs to reach a conclusion
Attribute special cause variation to the factors
Variation from a shift the experiment did not control gets assigned to whichever factor happened to change alongside it. Stability comes first, which is the same reason capability requires it.
stretch
I.A
In DMAIC, root causes are verified with data in which phase?
Define
Measure
Improve
Analyze

Analyze is where candidate causes are tested against data until the real ones are confirmed. Measure establishes the baseline and checks the measurement system; Improve acts on causes that Analyze has already verified.
std
I.A
Six Sigma describes an output as Y = f(X). The practical meaning is that:
Inspecting the output closely is the main way to improve it
Improving the output means controlling its inputs
Every input must be measured before any change can be made
The output is fixed by the specification and cannot move

Y = f(X) says the output is the result of its inputs, so lasting improvement comes from identifying the few X’s that matter and controlling them. Inspecting Y finds problems after they happen; it does not change the result.
std
I.B
Which is an example of the waste of motion?
Parts waiting in a queue between two operations
A worker walking to fetch a tool
Producing more parts than the customer ordered
Trucking parts between buildings
Motion is unnecessary movement of people. Waiting parts are the waste of waiting, producing ahead of demand is overproduction, and moving material between locations is transportation.
std
I.B
In lean thinking, value is defined by:
The quality standard the process meets
The process engineer’s design and drawings for the product
The cost accountant’s standard cost
The customer: what they are willing to pay for
Lean starts from the customer. A step adds value only if it changes the product in a way the customer wants and will pay for; everything else is a candidate for removal.
std
I.B
In a pull system, work on a part starts when:
The machine becomes free to start the next job
The raw material for the part arrives on site
A downstream step or customer signals a need
A forecast predicts the demand for next month
Pull means downstream demand authorizes upstream work, often through a kanban signal. Starting because a forecast says so, or because a machine or material is available, is push.
std
I.C
The person who runs the process day to day, and must keep the gain after the project closes, is the:
Team facilitator
Process owner
Master Black Belt
Black Belt
The process owner runs the process day to day and takes over the control plan at handover. The belts lead and coach the project, but they move on when it closes.
std
I.D.1
A team of people from purchasing, production and engineering, formed to solve a supplier problem, is best described as:
A virtual team
A natural work group
A cross-functional team
A self-directed team

Members drawn from several functions to work on one problem make a cross-functional team. A natural work group is people from the same area; self-directed and virtual describe how a team is run and where it meets.
std
I.D.1
A self-directed work team differs from other teams mainly in that it:
Meets only electronically and never in the same room
Disbands as soon as its single improvement project ends
Runs its own daily work with little supervision
Is always led by a trained Black Belt
A self-directed team plans, assigns and controls its own work. A team that disbands at the end of a project is a project team, and one that meets electronically is a virtual team.
std
I.D.1
Compared with a team that works in one location, the main added risk for a virtual team is:
No sponsor available to remove its obstacles
A smaller pool of people to choose members from
Weaker communication and trust between members
Lower technical skill among its members overall
Virtual teams lose the informal contact that builds trust and clears up misunderstandings, so they need more deliberate communication. They often have a wider pool of members, not a smaller one.
std
I.D.2
Team members argue about goals and roles and challenge the leader. The team is most likely in the stage of:
Performing
Storming
Norming
Forming
Conflict over direction, roles and leadership is the mark of storming. Forming is polite and uncertain, norming is when rules and roles settle, and performing is productive work.
std
I.D.2
While a team is forming, the leader helps most by:
Pressing for quick results
Keeping members from raising concerns that slow the team down
Giving clear direction on purpose, roles and ground rules
Stepping back and letting the team manage itself from the start
A forming team is uncertain and looks to the leader for direction. Stepping back suits a performing team; pressing for results or stifling concerns stores up conflict for later.
std
I.D.2
A team has agreed on its ground rules and roles, and members have begun to cooperate. It has reached:
Norming
Storming
Performing
Adjourning
Agreeing how to work together is norming. Performing comes next, when the team works with high productivity and little need for direction; adjourning is the close.
std
I.D.3
Multivoting is used to:
Reach a decision that every member fully agrees with
Cut a long list to the few the team favors
Assign the action items to individual team members
Rank causes by how often each one actually occurs
Multivoting gives each member several votes to spread across a list, which quickly cuts a brainstormed list to a shortlist. Ranking by frequency needs data, as in a Pareto chart.
std
I.D.3
Nominal group technique is especially useful when:
A decision is needed with no discussion at all
Data is already available to decide
A few strong voices could dominate the discussion
The decision belongs to the leader alone, after the meeting
Members generate ideas silently and then rank them individually, so quieter people have equal weight. It still includes clarifying discussion, so it is not a no-discussion method.
std
I.D.3
A decision reached by consensus means that:
More than half of the members voted for it
The leader decided after hearing everyone’s views
It was the first choice of every team member
All members can support it, first choice or not
Consensus is agreement to support the decision, not unanimity of first choices. A majority vote leaves a losing minority, and a leader deciding after consultation is a consultative decision.
std
I.D.4
To deliver a sensitive message to one stakeholder who strongly opposes the project, the best channel is usually:
The project newsletter
A notice board posting
A face-to-face conversation
An email to the distribution list
Sensitive messages to one person need a rich, two-way channel where reactions can be seen and answered. Broadcast channels suit routine updates to many people.
std
I.D.4
Two-way communication is preferred over one-way when:
Speed matters more than understanding
Understanding and buy-in must be confirmed
The audience is very large
The message is a routine weekly status update for the team
Two-way communication lets the receiver ask questions and the sender check understanding, which is what gaining buy-in needs. One-way is faster and suits routine messages to large audiences.
std
I.D.4
Active listening includes:
Planning your reply while the other person talks
Interrupting to correct mistakes
Paraphrasing to confirm understanding
Avoiding questions so as not to slow the speaker
Active listening means attending to the speaker and checking understanding, for example by restating their point. Planning a reply or interrupting means you are not listening.
std
I.E.1
A check sheet is used mainly to:
Rank the defect types in order of their importance to the customer
Collect tallied data consistently as it occurs
Show the relationship between two variables
Draw the steps and decisions of a process

A check sheet is a simple form for recording events as they happen, so data is consistent and easy to summarize. Ranking is the Pareto chart’s job, relationships the scatter diagram’s, and process steps the flowchart’s.
std
I.E.2
A process has three steps with first-pass yields of 98%, 95% and 90%. Its rolled throughput yield is about:

Rolled throughput yield is the product of the step yields: 0.98 × 0.95 × 0.90 = 0.838. Averaging the yields (94.3%) or taking the worst step (90%) overstates how many units get through every step right first time.
std
II.A.2
Which candidate is the best fit for a DMAIC project?
Installing software that has already been chosen
A recurring, costly defect with no known cause
A one-off complaint that has already been resolved
A known fix that is only waiting for budget approval
DMAIC suits a problem that keeps happening, whose cause is not known, and whose cost can be measured. A known fix is a just-do-it action, and an implementation or a one-off has nothing to analyze.
std
II.A.2
A project selection matrix scores candidate projects mainly on:
How many process steps each has
Benefit, effort and fit with business goals
Who proposed each project and how senior they are
How quickly each could be announced as a success
Selection weighs what a project would deliver against what it would take, and how well it serves the organization’s priorities. Who suggested it says nothing about whether it is worth doing.
std
II.A.3
A stakeholder with high influence over the project who currently opposes it should be:
Taken off the distribution list to avoid conflict
Engaged early, directly and in person
Left alone until the project has results to show
Kept informed through the general project newsletter
A powerful opponent can stop a project, so they need early, personal engagement. Waiting or relying on broadcast updates leaves their objections to grow unanswered.
std

Only the members of the project team and their manager
Only the customer who receives the product
Anyone affected by it or able to affect it
Only the managers who approve the project

Every task and decision in detail

The end user who buys the finished product
A customer who also buys from a competitor
A customer who complained
The person or department receiving your work

Demand leveling (heijunka)
Takt time variation

The cost-benefit analysis
The stakeholder analysis
The control chart
The FMEA

The single task that takes the longest time to complete
The project end date and nothing else
A key event in the schedule, with no duration
A line item in the approved project budget

Limiting contact with demanding stakeholders

The costliest tasks

8 days

Weighted mean
Midrange
Mean

Process A produces more defects

After collection, to record what was actually done
Only when the data collection is automated
Before any data is collected
By the sponsor rather than by the team itself

Collecting more data to average out the error
Replacing one of the two inspectors

Ratio
Ordinal
Interval

Shaft diameter in millimeters
Number of defects per unit
Machine number

Taking every nth item from the production line

Sampling only during the first hour of the shift

The process variation
The sample size needed
Transcription errors

The smallest increment the gauge can show
The variation between different operators
The variation in readings taken over a long period of time
Offset of the average reading from the true value

Reproducibility
Linearity

Parts that change size during the study

A worn gauge that gives inconsistent readings

The failure has a very severe effect

The failure happens often in the process

Address the severity 3 failure mode first
Treat the two as equal priority

Data shows the problem changes when that cause changes
It is the first answer given to “why?”

The report has been filed and signed

It seldom fixes why the process allowed the error

A nonconformity that has already occurred
Customer complaints only
Audit findings only
A potential nonconformity that has not yet occurred

Corrective action
Correction
Preventive action

A run chart of last month’s scrap
A Pareto chart of past complaints
A check sheet of defects found
An FMEA looks forward at how a product or process could fail and acts before it does. The other tools summarize problems that have already happened.

Poisson
Normal

Binomial
Poisson
Normal

A strong negative relationship
No relationship

A weak relationship that may be chance

Choosing the wrong test
An error in the measurement system

Continuous, small improvement involving everyone

The cause and effect diagram

Scatter diagram

Only random, everyday variation in the waits

15 minutes per unit
15 units per hour
4 minutes per unit
0.25 minutes per unit

Staff move patients through as fast as they can
A waiting room with more comfortable seating

A list of tools the team would like to try
The equipment the plant would like to buy
Cost of poor quality and complaint data
Ideas from whoever is free that month

They approve the budget and release resources
They are accountable for the process results
They supply expert knowledge of the software
Their acceptance decides if the screen is used

A subject matter expert
The process owner
An end user of the process
The project sponsor

They choose the statistical tools for the project
They will run the process after the team disbands
They are the customer who buys the final output
They are the only person allowed to collect data
The process owner is accountable for the process and must sustain the improvement once the project closes, so their early buy-in is essential. Choosing tools is the belt's job, not the owner's.

The test result report sent back to the doctor
Running the sample on the analyzer
The accuracy of the reported result
The nurse who draws and sends the sample

The supplier's invoice
The payment sent to the supplier
The clerk's approval of the invoice
The supplier who is paid

The menu the server uses
The guest who places the order at the table
An order ticket sent to the kitchen
Writing down the guest's choices
An output is what the process produces for its customer, here the ticket the kitchen works from. The menu is an input the server uses, and writing down the choices is a process step.

II.A.4
In a SIPOC for a company's payroll process, which is a customer?
The timesheets sent by supervisors
The vendor of the payroll software
Calculating hours and deductions
The employees who are paid
Customers receive the process outputs, and employees receive the paychecks. The software vendor supplies a tool to the process, which makes it a supplier rather than a customer.

Supply chain management is best described as:
Choosing the lowest-priced supplier for each purchased part
Coordinating flow from suppliers through to end customers
Managing the stockroom and inventory records of one plant
Negotiating long-term contracts with major customers only

Leave the supplier out of the plan until delivery
Shorten the Control phase to make up the lost time
Build the lead time into the schedule and risk plan
Order from the cheapest supplier to save on cost

Authorize the project and agree on its aim and limits
Record the root causes the team has verified
Document the control plan for the new process
List every task with its start and finish dates

Reduce scrap as much as is practical
Improve the scrap rate over the year
Eliminate the causes of scrap on the line
Cut scrap from 8% to 4% by June 30

A plan to tell operators early and directly
A larger sample size during the Measure phase
A more detailed process map of the line
A longer schedule for the Improve phase

A communication plan makes sure each group hears the right message from the right person at the right time, which builds support and avoids rumor-driven resistance. More data or more detailed maps do not change how people learn about the change.

Show each task as a bar across a calendar timeline
Rank the project risks by likelihood and impact
Split the deliverables into manageable pieces of work
Map the steps of the process being improved

Branches broken down from deliverables
Bars set against a calendar timeline
Nodes and arrows with no time scale
Points plotted between control limits

On a Gantt chart, today's date line falls halfway through a task's bar, but the shading shows the task is only 20% complete. The project leader should conclude that the task:
Is ahead of schedule and can be left alone
Is on the project's critical path
Has finished and can now be closed out
Is behind schedule and needs attention

After brainstorming, a team has 60 sticky notes of ideas about late deliveries. Which tool helps them sort the ideas into natural groups?
Affinity diagram
Tree diagram
Matrix chart
Activity network diagram

II.B.4
A team wants to show how strongly each of five customer requirements relates to each of four process steps. Which tool fits best?
Affinity diagram
Relations chart
Matrix chart
Tree diagram
A matrix chart sets two lists against each other and marks the strength of each pairing in the cells. A relations chart maps cause and effect among issues within one set, not between two lists.

A relations chart (interrelationship digraph) helps a team to:
Sort many ideas into a few themes
Find which issues drive the others
Break a goal into detailed actions
Schedule tasks along a critical path
Arrows drawn between issues show what causes what; issues with the most outgoing arrows are likely drivers. Sorting ideas into themes is the job of an affinity diagram.

Affinity diagram
Relations chart
Activity network diagram
Tree diagram

25 mm
625 mm
5 mm

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, which puts it back in the original units: the square root of 25 is 5 mm. Halving the variance (12.5) is a common slip, but variance and standard deviation are linked by squaring, not by a factor of two.

III.B.1

Any payment made after the invoice due date
The invoice log in the accounts payable system
Weekly, extracted each Friday by the analyst
Days from invoice receipt to the payment date
The data source says where the data comes from, here the accounts payable system. The other entries are the operational definition of late, the collection frequency and the measure itself.

How often the data will be gathered and for how long
Where the data comes from, such as a machine or a database
How the data will be gathered, such as a check sheet or report
Exactly what counts as a defect and how it is measured
The method is how the data is gathered: a check sheet, a system report, a survey or a gauge reading. Where it comes from is the data source, and how often is the frequency.

The fill weight lacks an operational definition
Samples should come from a different data source
Start-of-shift samples are the least accurate ones
Sampling is too infrequent to show drift in a shift

The reason is qualitative and the minutes are quantitative
Both are quantitative because every call can be counted
The reason is quantitative and the minutes are qualitative
Both are qualitative because they describe the same call

The number of patients who miss their appointments each week is:
Continuous data
Ordinal data
Discrete data
Nominal data

Ratio
Interval
Ordinal
Nominal

Zero degrees does not mean there is no temperature
Its values can be ranked from colder to hotter
The gaps between the degrees are not equal
Temperatures can only be recorded in whole degrees

Oven temperature in degrees Fahrenheit
Weight of a casting in kilograms
Customer rating from one to five stars
Part number stamped on the casting

A short written or online survey
One-on-one interviews with each patient
A check sheet kept at the discharge desk
A checklist for the discharging nurses

Reach more people at a lower cost per answer
Let the team ask follow-up questions on reasons
Give numeric results that are easier to analyze
Remove any influence of the interviewer on answers

A checklist
A control chart
A check sheet
A Pareto chart

A check sheet
A process map
A control chart
A checklist

Number all invoices and pick 30 by random number
Take the 30 invoices at the top of the file
Pick the 30 that look most likely to have errors
Take every 20th invoice, starting with the first

How close the average reading is to the true value
How closely repeated readings agree with each other
How the readings change as the gauge ages over time
How the bias changes across the range of the gauge

Accurate but not precise
Neither accurate nor precise
Both accurate and precise
Precise but not accurate

Linearity
Stability
Reproducibility
Repeatability

To skip collecting baseline data on the process
To set the specification limits for the product
To know the data reflects the process, not the gauge
To prove that the process is in statistical control

One operator measures each of many different parts just once
Several operators each measure the same parts more than once
Each operator measures a different set of parts more than once
The gauge is checked against a master standard after calibration

Sort
Shine
Sustain
Set in order

Remove all of the items that are not needed for the current work
Give each needed item a marked home at its point of use
Clean the equipment so that leaks and wear are easy to spot early
Check each month that the area still meets the agreed standard

Sorting
Setup reduction
Inspection
Kanban

Run a kaizen blitz to redesign the whole layout of the cell
Audit the cell every month and post the scores on a board
Agree common rules, checklists and visual standards

Sustain
Sort
Shine
Set in order

Is required by the company's own internal procedures and policies
Changes the product or service in a way the customer values
Is done at a step that is staffed by skilled, well-paid workers
Is done quickly, correctly and without any errors or rework

Value-added, because it is required by the health regulations

Non-value-added but necessary, so keep it to a minimum
Value-added, because trained lab staff are the ones who do it

Motion
Transportation
Overproduction
Waiting

How likely the cause or failure mode is to happen
How serious the effect is for the customer or user
How likely current controls are to catch the failure
How many process steps the failure mode will affect

The defects found at final inspection last year
The ways that step could fail to do its job
The operators who will run that step on each shift
The cost of the equipment that is used at that step

It proves which cause is responsible by timing each of the steps
It ranks the causes of the problem from the most to the least common
It shows where in the flow the problem starts and what feeds into it
It removes the need to collect any further data about the problem

Recognize the team and close out the problem
Change systems to prevent the problem recurring
Put interim containment actions in place

Rank the root causes by how often each one has occurred in the past
Measure how strongly two of the process variables are related
Draw each step of the procedure in the order in which it is done

That cause is a likely root cause to investigate first
That cause has been proven to cause all three defects
The other three causes can be dropped from the study
The chart should be redrawn as a Pareto chart

Containing the problem at the line
